title: For adolescent girls in northern Nigeria, digital-literacy gains depend on safe-space delivery and implementation fidelity rather than technology alone
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11445, Safe Spaces to Digital Spaces: Short-Term Impacts of Life Skills and Digital Literacy Training for Adolescent Girls in Nigeria, September 2026
geography: Northern Nigeria, including Kaduna, Kano, and Katsina; adolescent girls in senior secondary schools, school delivery systems, families, and local communities

denominator.unit: school-based evaluation of life-skills and digital-literacy interventions for adolescent girls in northern Nigeria

curriculum_knowledge.value: girls in treated schools show modest improvements in curriculum-related knowledge twelve months after intervention

school_retention.value: the intervention shows no effect on school retention at the reported follow-up

social_emotional.value: the intervention shows no effect on socio-emotional skills at the reported follow-up

observations.method: World Bank evaluation of school-based life-skills training delivered in safe spaces, alone or combined with digital-literacy training, with follow-up twelve months after intervention.
observations.uncertainty: The results are short-term and context-specific; no effect at twelve months does not establish no longer-term effect, and the evaluation does not show that all implementation components had equal exposure.
observations.subgroup: Adolescent girls in northern Nigerian secondary schools, girls facing early marriage or limited schooling, and students with different school, household, and technology access conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Knowledge gains may be valuable even without immediate retention or socio-emotional changes; retention depends on household costs, distance, safety, school quality, and norms beyond a classroom intervention.

denominator.unit: combined life-skills and digital-literacy intervention evaluation

digital_skill_effect.value: adding digital-literacy training improved digital skills in the state where it had been fully implemented by midline

fidelity.value: the result underscores implementation fidelity as a condition of technology-based programme impact

delivery_capacity.value: school systems in low-resource settings may face delivery constraints that determine whether digital training is actually received

observations.method: Comparative evaluation of schools receiving life-skills training alone or combined with digital-literacy training, with attention to state-level implementation timing and completeness.
observations.uncertainty: The evidence does not identify which specific delivery constraint drove the heterogeneous result, nor whether digital skills persisted or translated into education, health, or employment outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Girls in states with different implementation completeness, schools with different infrastructure and teacher capacity, and students with unequal access to devices, power, and connectivity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technology can be effective when embedded in functioning delivery systems; a weak result may reflect timing or implementation rather than limits of digital literacy itself.

intervention_sequence.value: the programme links safe-space life skills with digital literacy to address education, health, and economic outcomes

agency_context.value: safe spaces are positioned as a delivery environment for girls' life skills and later digital participation

scale_condition.value: the study highlights delivery capacity as critical to scaling technology-based programmes in low-resource settings

observations.method: World Bank intervention evaluation and implementation interpretation for adolescent-girls education and digital-literacy programming.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not establish that safe spaces alone cause digital participation, safety, agency, or labour-market outcomes, and it does not measure every social norm or household constraint.
observations.subgroup: Girls with different exposure to safe school environments, early marriage pressure, household responsibilities, social norms, disability, and digital access.
observations.counterinterpretation: A safe-space model can create belonging and trusted learning, but it may remain bounded if schools lack power, devices, trained facilitators, teacher support, or pathways into continued education and work.

boundary: This record adds a safe-space-to-digital-participation route for adolescent girls, linking life skills, digital literacy, implementation fidelity, school retention, socio-emotional outcomes, and delivery capacity. It does not establish long-term empowerment, causal employment or health effects, universal digital access, or that technology alone changes social norms.
